content.title: Wetland Restoration Project
content.summary: The wetland restoration project at Majestic View Park is currently focused on the removal of invasive Russian Olive trees, which consume significant amounts of water and harm native species. This phase aims to enhance the ecosystem by improving water quality and expanding habitats for wildlife, with plans for replanting native trees supported by community donations. The project, backed by over $320,000 in grants, addresses issues like silt buildup and invasive vegetation to preserve and restore the wetland's biodiversity.
content.body:
## UPDATE! Current Phase: Russian Olive Removal

To minimize water loss and improve habitat, Russian Olive trees will be removed from critical portions of the watershed west of the Majestic View Park and Nature Center. Russian Olive trees ([pictured below](/ImageRepository/Document?documentID=6693)) can drink 75 to 150 gallons of water a day. Although pretty, these light sage-colored invasive trees offer little-to-no benefit to local flora and fauna. In fact, they are detrimental to many native species and will out-compete them.

As these trees get removed in the coming months, the approach might seem aggressive, leaving areas of sparse vegetation. This temporary phase is a very important step in improving the entirety of the ecosystem.

[View enlarged map of Russian Olive removal](/ImageRepository/Document?documentID=6750)

![Map and photos showing 5.6-acre Russian olive removal zones at Majestic View Park.](/ImageRepository/Document?documentId=6750)

## Help replant the wetlands by donating a tree

Do you want to support Majestic View Park ecosystem and help bring back a treed beautiful view?

**Consider donating to the Friends of Majestic View to pay for a regionally appropriate tree** to be planted in the wetland area where Russian Olive trees will be removed. A tree sapling costs approximately $20 per tree but you can donate as little or as much as you want! Just make sure to add a comment and type ‘Tree’ so we know it is for this project.

### [Donate a Tree](https://www.majesticviewfriends.org/take-action "Friends of Majestic View Donation")

## Wetland restoration project background

The Majestic View Wetlands are primarily located in the wildlife resting areas of the 80-acre park. These emergent marshy habitats are home to a variety of plants and wildlife, some of which are invasive and problematic. To preserve the quality and the beauty of the wetlands and lake, and to support as many native species as possible, we are completing projects to conserve the water and revegetate native plants.

### Project Goals:

- Improve wetland habitat and water quality.
- Expand existing wetlands to provide more habitat for wildlife.
- Increase biodiversity.
- Prolong the existence of the wetland habitat, delaying succession into a cattail marsh.

![Aerial Russian Olive Trees in Majestic View Park](/ImageRepository/Document?documentId=6693)

## The Problem

- The lake has less water than historical levels, and less water capacity. Over the past fifty years, the**lake has filled in with silt from erosion and road runoff**, reducing the water capacity of the lake and leading to cattail encroachment. Without intervention, Oberon Lake will completely fill with silt & cattails, eliminating most, if not all, aquatic habitat.
- **Invasive vegetation is degrading habitat and drinking up storm water,** reducing the amount of water available for native plants and wildlife in the wetlands and lake. Invasive vegetation supports fewer species of wildlife by reducing preferred food and/or shelter sources. Without intervention the habitat will continue to lose biodiversity and may potentially experience periods with no water reaching the lower marsh.

## The Solution

- **Partner with experts**, such as Ducks Unlimited, U.S. Fish and Wildlife, Colorado Parks & Wildlife, Colorado Water Conservation Board, Volunteers of Outdoor Colorado, Majestic View Friends, and others to determine the best course of action to achieve long-term ecosystem health.
  - Thanks to our partners, this project has received over $320,000 in grants and in-kind support for restoration work.
- **Remove noxious weeds**, such as Russian Olive trees (Class B) and Teasel (Class B), and replanting native vegetation such as Swamp Milkweed, Marsh Aster, Willows, and more.
- **Prevent further silt build-up** in the lake by installing dikes with maintenance spillways in the watershed upstream of the wetland areas.

## Timeline

- This is a multi-year restorative process, with stages affected by migration seasons, weather, funding, and volunteer availability.
- With the support from various grants, we anticipate most of the disturbance being complete by 2027. Further monitoring and revegetation effort will continue for the next 5-10 years.

![](/ImageRepository/Document?documentId=6692)

Wetland Restoration Timeline showing that we are at the "Russian Olive Tree Removal" phase of the project.

## Common Questions

### What will happen to wildlife?

By working in phases, we will allow time for wildlife to adapt and move around the disturbed areas. Populations will continue to be monitored, with the expectation of long-term benefits to wildlife through improved and more diverse habitat.

### How are we monitoring?

Staff and volunteers conduct visual observations and bio blitzes, in addition to wildlife cameras that operate 24/7 to observe wildlife and their behavior.

We periodically check the water quality and depth, measuring bacteria overgrowth, temperature, PH, salinity, etc. We also check for indicator species ꟷ invertebrates that have a known tolerance to pollutants ꟷ to help determine water quality.

### Why are we intervening?

Wetlands are critically important ecosystems – yet fewer than half of these areas remain. They provide habitat for animals, clean water, remove pollutants from the soil, reduce flood impacts, and more.

Historically, this area was primarily short-grass prairie with seasonal ponds and a few trees near low-lying marshy areas, allowing a larger variety of species to use this area for resting, nesting, and migration. As humans have removed prairie and temporary pond habitats, wildlife populations have suffered greatly. Human infrastructure has negatively impacted water quality and introduced species have led to a loss in biodiversity.

In the 1960s & 1970s, many landowners planted Russian Olive trees around their houses as fast-growing, easy to spread windbreaks. These trees have spread and now are found throughout the wetland. By replacing these trees with more regionally-appropriate plants, we will undo some of the damage done and restore this important ecosystem.

### Will this impact the views?

While there may be a noticeable change in the landscape with fewer Russian Olive trees and the removal of some of the cattails, this disturbance is temporary. As we work towards long-term restoration, the views should remain wild, tranquil, and full of flora and fauna. As native vegetation fills in over the next several years, there will be a change in vegetation but still abundant nature to maintain the views and habitat structure for wildlife.

### How will the park change?

As stated above, the changes will be noticeable at first with fewer trees and cattails, but a larger, more exciting change is on the horizon! With this project completed there is a potential for additional wetland habitats that will bring in more wildlife and native plants that will revegetate the area. Below is a picture of where that potential wetland habitat will occur and where the invasive Russian Olives will be removed and replanted with native trees.

![Aerial View of Majestic View Park with Potential Changes](/ImageRepository/Document?documentId=6694)

## Comparing 1963 to 2019, Many Changes Over Time

Even just 60 years ago, the landscape looked very different. While we recognize ecosystems change over time and will likely look very different in another 60 years, we are hoping to slow those changes. Preserving water and reducing human impacts on the wetlands help our plants and wildlife adapt and hopefully continue to thrive in our community for many more years to come. (Photo on left taken by aircraft in 1963, photo on right from Google aerial imagery circa 2019).

![Left: 1963 with very few homes and a lake. Right: 2021 with many homes and a much smaller lake ](/ImageRepository/Document?documentId=4888)
